item.title: CDC director responds to Democratic lawmakers' growing oversight of her tenure
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
NEW YORK (AP) — Three months into her tenure as head of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Dr. Erica Schwartz is being investigated by House Democrats, facing a call to resign, and drawing ire from both within and outside the agency. What's been happening at the nation's top public health agency has alarmed outside health professionals. It also has alienated staff, leaving morale as bad as ever, employees say. Schwartz, 54, took the helm of the CDC at a very challenging time: the worst U.S. measles epidemic in more than three decades, a large dengue fever outbreak in Florida and the fastest-growing overseas Ebola outbreak in history. She reports to U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who is a longtime critic of vaccines and federal public health policy and who played a role in decimating CDC staffing last year. “She has a tough job, at a tough time, and a tough boss,” said Noel Brewer, a University of North Carolina public health professor. In an interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday, Schwartz defended her work, saying she's trying to restore trust in the CDC — including by changing how measles-associated deaths are being reported. She said some of the criticisms are based on misperceptions and argued she is making progress on her goals. “I do understand why people have concerns," Schwartz told the AP from her home in Naples, Florida. “Have I made mistakes? Certainly. But I'm here to work on the behalf of the American people.” Some experts say she has made the situation worse. And critics are seizing on the Pan American Health Organization’s declaration last week that measles is continuously spreading here, marking the re-establishment of a public health threat that was eliminated in the last century. “I have no confidence that she will do what it takes to course-correct at the CDC, and she should resign immediately,” said U.S. Sen. Michael Bennet, a Colorado Democrat. Schwartz has an impressive resume When President Donald Trump nominated Schwartz to be the next CDC director in April, he called her “a STAR!” on social media. She holds both medical and law degrees. She was chief medical officer for the U.S. Coast Guard, where she oversaw 41 clinics and 150 sick bays. She served as deputy surgeon general in the U.S. Public Health Service, helping to lead uniformed medical and health professionals posted at the CDC and government health agencies. Many public health leaders were cautiously optimistic, noting the CDC badly needed steady leadership after enduring more than a year of turmoil and months of being led by interim directors. Schwartz was the third Trump nominee for CDC director in less than 18 months. The first was a former Florida congressman whose nomination was pulled an hour before a Senate confirmation hearing. The second was Susan Monarez, who won Senate approval but then was ousted less than a month into the job when Trump administration officials said she was not aligned with the president’s agenda. Under Kennedy, the agency has seen around 30% of its staff leave, mostly through layoffs, resignations and retirements. At her nomination hearing , Schwartz pledged “radical transparency” to rebuild public trust in the agency, which she noted declined during the COVID-19 pandemic and which has eroded further under Kennedy. “I will always stand on science and speak the truth, even in difficult moments,” she testified. Meanwhile, public misperceptions about vaccines have persisted. A recent Annenberg Public Policy Center survey found that about 1 in 6 Americans said they believed that “vaccines given to children for diseases like measles, mumps and rubella cause autism” — even though dozens of studies have determined there’s no causal link. Roughly another 1 in 5 said they didn’t know whether it was true. Schwartz hasn’t held a news conference Schwartz started at the Atlanta-based agency in mid-August. A week later, she held her first “all hands” staff meeting , during which she promised to advocate for the agency and said she wouldn’t hesitate to disagree with Kennedy — but only privately. Some say that’s when their optimism for Schwartz began to fade. “I don’t have a clear sense of what is important to her, what are her red lines,” one CDC health scientist told the AP. “If we’re talking about radical transparency,” it is appropriate to know on what issues and what messaging she will not compromise, the scientist added. The employee spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of retribution. Asked about that assessment, Schwartz said: “I would never do anything unethical or illegal. ... That is a red line.” Despite that transparency pledge, CDC and HHS officials for months would not release Schwartz’s salary — even though it is public information. Schwartz is paid about $375,000 a year, CDC officials finally told the AP this week, above the typical range for previous CDC directors. So far she also has been less visible than some predecessors. She has not held any news conferences, and has not used her bully pulpit to try to persuade more Americans to get vaccinations — including for measles, the flu and COVID-19. Schwartz told the AP that, concerning measles, she doesn't believe a federal health official on TV will sway most of the unvaccinated. But with the nation experiencing its worst measles epidemic in decades, many public health and medical leaders say Schwartz should be strongly urging Americans to get vaccinated. “I hope to see her display independence from the vaccine rhetoric and challenges that have been part of this administration,” said Dr. Wendy Armstrong, president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. “I don’t think we have seen that yet.” Kennedy continues to back Schwartz. The Health and Human Services Department issued a statement in response to Associated Press queries, quoting Kennedy as saying she had his full support. “Dr. Schwartz brings the judgment to make hard decisions and the courage to see them through. She is reforming CDC and sharpening its focus on its core mission: protecting Americans from disease,” the statement said. Congressional Democrats are launching investigations Some Democratic legislators accuse Schwartz and Kennedy of downplaying measles. Kennedy has challenged health officials’ accounts of measles deaths. And the CDC has stopped quickly relaying state reports of measles deaths. It adopted a new policy requiring the review of death certificates, which has resulted in CDC counting only about half the measles-associated deaths that states are reporting. Schwartz said that was her decision, and stemmed from her desire to have a uniform definition of what counts as a measles death. Democrats on the House Energy & Commerce Committee have questioned why CDC changed the policy. “As the crisis worsens, we are concerned that you continue to direct an effort at CDC to downplay the outbreak and artificially reduce the number of deaths that CDC reports,” according to a statement from Reps. Frank Pallone Jr. of New Jersey, Diana DeGette of Colorado and Yvette Clarke of New York. “We are expanding our investigation to examine the threats your actions pose to Americans’ health and whether changes to your statutory authority are required,” they added. The statement followed a briefing at which Schwartz was supposed to answer congressional staffers' questions about the measles data. The committee leaders described Schwartz as unresponsive and, at times, misleading. Schwartz argued that she was “fully transparent. And I am really concerned that they think there is more to the story. There isn't.” CDC employees see little sign of progress The AP interviewed eight current CDC workers about Schwartz's tenure. They all spoke on condition of anonymity, saying they feared retribution for speaking frankly about what’s going on within the agency. Some said they never had high expectations. Others said they initially were hopeful but lost confidence, some of them blaming her handling of the measles death count. One said it’s still too early to judge her. Several said they had hoped for more improvements and stability. Announcements about leadership appointees coming, going and changing titles have continued in a blur, the employees told the AP. Some mentioned Caroline DeBerry, a former vice president at a conservative think tank and author of independently published novels including one titled “Esther: The Woman Who Didn’t Know Her Place.” DeBerry got a job as acting director of communications, starting in August. Employees said she gained notoriety within the agency when all CDC website updates ground to a halt while awaiting her approval. Asked about it, Schwartz said: “There was a bit of clunkiness that happened one day.” She also said DeBerry is on “terminal leave” and her last day will be in December, but did not immediately offer additional detail. None of the agency veterans interviewed by the AP said they have spoken with Schwartz. But some said they had seen her around the CDC campus accompanied by a group of security guards. Security has been a sensitive topic at CDC, especially since an August 2025 shooting outside the entrance of CDC’s main campus. A Georgia man who had blamed the COVID-19 vaccine for making him depressed and suicidal opened fire, killing a police officer and spraying bullets into 150 windows . (The slain officer, David Rose, is widely held up as a hero by CDC employees, and some expressed irritation that Schwartz referred to him as “Officer Stone” during a recent health summit appearance.) Dr. Tom Frieden, who served as CDC director in the Obama administration, said he occasionally had an escort outside the CDC campus after he received death threats. But Schwartz moves with a large security team inside CDC, and agency staffers said they don’t recall seeing that before. “It feels like they’re afraid of us,” one health scientist said. Schwartz acknowledged that early in her time at CDC, she walked the halls accompanied by about a half dozen guards at the recommendation of security leadership. The security details have been reduced to one plainclothes guard, she said. Confusion over the publication of scientific reports A directive about research publications shows just how far apart CDC staff feel from the political leadership. Two CDC scientists told the AP that they were directed in a recent meeting to stop submitting their research to journals run by organizations that have sued Kennedy. The prohibition would cover Pediatrics, one of the most-cited journals for doctors who specialize in children’s medical care, and Clinical Infectious Diseases, a highly regarded publication for doctors focused on germs. The scientists said the directive was clearly stated but not written down in a memo or email. HHS and CDC officials are adamant that neither Kennedy nor any other HHS or CDC official ever issued such a directive. At the health summit, Schwartz acknowledged that CDC employees have lost trust in the political appointees who have been put in charge of the agency, “and I’m trying to earn that trust every day.” She talked about work going on to stabilize the agency’s leadership and develop a “strategic hiring plan” for 2027. CDC employees look around and see burned-out colleagues. “I think everyone is just exhausted,” one health scientist said. “There’s just a sense that we can’t go on like this anymore.” ___ The Associated Press’ health and science coverage receives financial support from the AP Fund for Journalism and private foundations. AP is solely responsible for all content. Find AP’s standards for working with philanthropies, a list of supporters and funded coverage areas at AP.org . item.title: CIA and intel director’s office reportedly hit by hack affecting unclassified information
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The main entrance of CIA headquarters in Langley, Virginia, on July 8, 2022. - Kevin Lamarque/Reuters/File The CIA and Office of the Director of National Intelligence suffered an apparent hack affecting unclassified information, four sources familiar with the matter told CNN. The intrusion hit a system the agencies draw on​ for open-source intelligence analysis, one of the sources said. The full extent of the breach was unclear, but officials emphasized that no classified information was affected. “There have been no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems,” an ODNI official told CNN. The CIA declined to comment. It is not immediately clear when the hack occurred, who was responsible for it, or if it has been resolved. The Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), which oversees 17 US intelligence agencies, including the CIA, has in recent years invested in open-source intelligence work, which is often unclassified. The apparent intrusion, which the New York Times first reported , is the latest in a string of cybersecurity incidents or tech outages that have rattled the US government and private sector. The incident does not appear to be related to an apparent hack of the FBI’s nationwide criminal information database, two of the sources said, which CNN first reported on Friday. The hacking incidents have coincided with a series of unrelated high-profile tech outages affecting banks, the National Security Agency and the FAA’s air traffic control system that have rattled Americans’ confidence in the technology that underpins their lives. All flights nationwide were grounded for hours earlier this month after a massive systems failure, leading to thousands of flights being delayed or canceled. The Federal Aviation Administration traced the problem to a single router in Arkansas. Separately, an outage affecting Microsoft products left people around the world unable to access staples of work life like Outlook email accounts and Teams meetings. But it’s the disruption at the NSA, the US’ signals intelligence spy agency, and intrusions at the FBI and CIA that have national security officials on alert. The highly classified network that the NSA uses for its internal communications went down for multiple days last week, CNN first reported . The apparent cause was a software update gone wrong and not a cyberattack, the nation’s spy chief Jay Clayton said. A critical Georgia facility that supports signals intelligence and cybersecurity operations focused on the Middle East, where the US is currently engaged in a war with Iran was also impacted, CNN reported . The NSA’s most sensitive and important intelligence-gathering systems were unaffected by the outage, and by Friday, the outage was resolved. The software vulnerabilities that the NSA was addressing are just a handful in a slew of new vulnerabilities that artificial intelligence has been able to locate. Cybersecurity experts say government agencies and companies alike are discovering a spate of new software bugs in their systems thanks to AI, prompting a rush to fix them and sometimes mistakes along the way. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/24/politics/cia-odni-hack-unclassified-information

item.title: Democrats flip Tennessee's 4th District, giving the party 259 House seats
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Democrats' House majority grew to at least 259 seats on Tuesday — the party's largest since 1992 — after Victoria Broderick narrowly defeated Republican incumbent Scott DesJarlais in Tennessee's 4th Congressional District. Broderick's victory comes two days after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican incumbent Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina's 5th District. Foxx has held the seat since 2005. The final balance of power in the Senate was settled on Nov. 17, when Mary Peltola's victory in Alaska gave Democrats their ninth flipped seat of the 2026 midterm elections, the most in nearly 70 years . When the next Congress takes office in early January, the party will hold its largest Senate majority since 2011, with 56 seats to the GOP's 44. Though very few races remain unresolved, the dust has mostly settled on Democrats' 2026 landslide. Their sweeping victories in the U.S. House, Senate and statehouses nationwide add up to the biggest "blue wave" since Watergate . The question now is what Democrats plan to do with their newfound power. Last week, the party nominated New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker, putting him on track to be the first Black American to wield the gavel. With a majority that could top out at 260 seats, Jeffries will have enormous leeway to send new legislation to the Senate while also blocking parts of President Trump's agenda, investigating his administration and possibly even impeaching him (again) . On the Senate side, Chuck Schumer of New York faces a challenge from Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen for majority leader. Senate Democrats will vote by secret ballot on Dec. 1, and the winner needs 28 votes. Schumer has 15 public backers to Van Hollen's five, with 34 senators undeclared, according to The Hill's count . Schumer says he has the votes. Van Hollen said Sunday on NBC's "Meet the Press" that "we're north of 15 and momentum is in our direction." Trump weighed in Sunday morning. "It is going to be very hard for me to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader," he wrote on Truth Social , two days after saying he could make deals with Schumer and Jeffries. Whoever wins will control which bills reach the floor, when votes occur and which judges and appointees are confirmed. Among the priorities under discussion on both sides of the aisle: reinstating Affordable Care Act subsidies that expired under the previous Republican Congress; reversing nearly $1 trillion in recent GOP Medicaid cuts; expanding Medicare by lowering the eligibility age and adding vision, hearing and dental coverage; addressing the high prices of groceries and other goods by blocking Trump's global tariffs and restoring congressional power over trade policy; cutting off Iran war funding; and launching investigations of ICE, presidential pardons, political pressure on federal law enforcement, the Epstein files and the Trump family's business dealings. As for impeachment, Rep. Jamie Raskin, a Democrat from Maryland who is set to chair the House Judiciary Committee, told Punchbowl that it's a "critical tool in the constitutional toolbox" — but far from a sure thing. "We will not hesitate to use it if we think that the benefits exceed the costs," Raskin said. "But the one thing everybody's well aware of is that impeachment trials and impeachment motions soak up a lot of energy and oxygen." Despite their sizable House and Senate majorities, Democrats will be limited in what legislation they can pass into law. Trump still has veto power, and Senate Republicans still hold enough seats to filibuster most bills. Meanwhile, many incoming Democratic lawmakers (like Peltola) are relative moderates representing red states and districts — meaning the party will have to calibrate its approach carefully to keep them on board and maximize its chances of winning the 2028 elections. Beyond Washington, D.C., Democrats will now control the governorship and both legislative houses in six new states: Arizona, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Nevada, Michigan and Minnesota. They will also hold the majority in a dozen new statehouse chambers. As a result, the party will have more opportunities to experiment with new policy ideas, approve congressional maps, influence election procedures, fill Senate vacancies and help a new generation of governors build executive experience ahead of future presidential elections. It's even possible that state Democratic leaders could change the way we elect our next president by sidestepping the Electoral College and preventing candidates from winning the White House without winning the popular vote . How many Senate seats did Democrats win? Democrats came into the midterms needing a net gain of four seats to win back the Senate. To do that, they had to defend a handful of potentially vulnerable swing-state seats while also flipping at least a few seats in historically red states. That's exactly what happened. Republican efforts to flip blue seats in Michigan, Georgia, Minnesota and New Hampshire all came up well short. Meanwhile, Democrats won nine GOP-held seats in Mississippi, Maine, Texas, South Carolina, Ohio, North Carolina, Iowa, Kansas and Alaska. Only two incumbent Republican senators in competitive races were able to win reelection: Florida's Ashley Moody and Nebraska's Pete Ricketts. The last undecided race was called Nov. 17, as Mary Peltola defeated incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan to become the first Alaska Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate since 2008. Peltola secured just over 50% of the vote, narrowly clearing the threshold required to win without triggering Alaska's unique ranked choice voting system. Democrats will enter 2027 with 56 seats in the Senate . How many House seats did Democrats win? So far, Democrats have won at least 258 U.S. House seats , far more than the 218 they needed for a majority. That includes 48 red-to-blue flips, for a net gain of 45 seats. That is four more than the 40 they picked up in Trump's first midterm in 2018. Democrats' 14-point victory in the House popular vote is the largest in any midterm since 1974. Races that were too close to call on Election Night have been decided in the days that followed. On Sunday, the AP called North Carolina's 5th District for Democrat Chuck Hubbard, a former journalist, over Rep. Virginia Foxx, who has held the seat since 2005. Cook Political Report had rated the seat likely Republican, and Foxx won it by nearly 19 points in 2024. Foxx, who requested a recount last week, said in a statement that she had called Hubbard to congratulate him. She has already filed to run for the seat again in 2028, WFMY reported . Democrats picked up another flip on Tuesday when Broderick was named the winner in Tennessee's 4th District, defeating DesJarlais by just a few hundred votes. Broderick will be the lone Democrat among the Volunteer State's House caucus. Where things stand in the undecided House races Three U.S. House races remain unresolved. Two are in Louisiana, where the top two finishers in the 5th and 6th Districts will meet in a Dec. 12 runoff. The last remaining House race that will be decided based on votes cast on Election Day is in Minnesota's 1st District, where Democrat Jake Johnson leads GOP Rep. Brad Finstad by just over 300 votes. Finstad requested a recount , which runs Nov. 30 to Dec. 3. The state canvassing board will certify the race Dec. 8. How many governorships did Democrats win? Republican governors have outnumbered their Democratic counterparts for the last 15 years straight (and for 26 of the last 30 years overall). But this year, Democrats have reversed the "governor gap," flipping six governorships in Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Nevada, Alaska and Georgia to bring their total to 30 — the party's first gubernatorial majority since 2011. On Thursday, Democrats also held onto Kansas, where voters elected Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher to become the Sunflower State's fourth woman governor ever. She defeated Republican Ty Masterson, the state's Senate president. "Kansans have sent a clear message that they want to keep our state moving forward," Holscher said in a video posted online Tuesday. "The work of preparing to lead has already begun." The AP called Alaska's governor race for Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins early Saturday. He won a majority of first-choice votes, so no ranked-choice count was needed. He will be the state's first Democratic governor since Tony Knowles left office in 2002, and he takes office Dec. 7. How many state legislatures did Democrats win? Democrats' gains were also seen at the state level. They flipped more than 500 state legislative seats across the country and turned a total of 12 legislative chambers blue. That includes three states where they flipped both chambers: Arizona, New Hampshire and Wisconsin. After Election Day's results, Democrats will control the House, Senate and governorship in Arizona for the first time since 1966. Democrats also secured a "trifecta" in Wisconsin. They'll hold both legislative chambers in New Hampshire, but the governorship in the Granite State will remain in Republican hands. Democrats regained trifectas in Minnesota, Michigan and Pennsylvania by clinching majorities in the lone GOP-led chamber in their states. They flipped a single chamber in Georgia, North Carolina and Texas, ensuring that Democratic governors in those states won't face unified Republican opposition within their state legislatures. Where things stand in the undecided state legislative races As of Monday morning, only three state legislative chambers — the North Carolina Senate and both chambers in Alaska — remained undecided, according to the AP. A recount is possible in North Carolina, where Senate control hinges on one race. item.title: One every 4 minutes: 720,000 Russian soldiers killed in Ukraine war, new data suggests
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A monument to the dead overlooks a massive burial site of Russian soldiers in the rural Volga region of Kostroma, Russia, on October 20, 2025. - Andrey Borodulin/AFP/Getty Images Almost three-quarters of a million Russian soldiers have been killed since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, equating to roughly one death every four minutes, analysis based on leaked official data has revealed. Russian opposition outlets Mediazona and Meduza reported on Monday that by the end of September, 490,000 Russian troops had been confirmed dead by Russia’s statistical bureau, Rosstat. But accounting for time lags in reporting and including troops who have been reported as missing in action – and are most likely dead – Russian fatalities jump to more than 720,000 since the start of the war, according to the two outlets. That is a staggering number that surpasses Russia’s death toll from the Soviet war in Afghanistan in the 1980s and both Chechen wars in the 1990s and early 2000s – and which the Kremlin has long tried to keep secret. Rosstat stopped publishing demographic data in 2025 to disguise the rising death toll from the war. Mediazona and Meduza, as well as other outlets, obtained the official data after two pro-Ukrainian hacker groups, Cyber ​​Partisans of Belarus and Silent Crow, managed to breach Rosstat’s servers earlier this month. CNN cannot independently verify the figures, but the leaked data on confirmed deaths alone corroborates earlier estimates by analysts and Western intelligence – which now appear to fall far short of the likely real death toll. Mediazona and Meduza have long been keeping a tally of Russian losses, based mostly on inheritance documents, death notices and other publicly available documents. Ukrainian servicemen fire a self-propelled howitzer towards Russian positions in eastern Ukraine on December 28, 2022. - Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty Images But the leaked Rosstat data allowed the media outlets to go a step further, using the same methods and calculations normally employed by actuaries estimating risks and insurance premiums. By analyzing discrepancies between reported death dates and death registration dates, and by comparing these to search notices published by relatives, the reporters were able to extrapolate the number of deaths that have occurred but have not yet been reported to be somewhere around 230,000. Mediazona has kept a tally of troops identified as missing by their relatives from 2023. That database contains 160,000 individuals and almost all of them are likely dead. Mediazona said that based on its reporting, the rate of survival among those reported missing only around 10%. unknown content item - The data shared by Silent Crow showed that the war was the fourth most common cause of death in Russia since the start of the full-scale invasion, after heart diseases; Covid; and stroke and other vascular conditions. It also confirms what has long been suspected – that the losses are not spread evenly across Russia, with poorer areas and ethnic minorities suffering significantly higher casualty rates. In addition, an analysis by the NEST Centre, a think tank that also obtained the data, revealed the scale of Russia’s recruitment of foreign fighters. It identified 6,947 records of foreign nationals killed in Ukraine – the majority of them from the central Asian countries of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Turkmenistan. Like Russia, Ukraine doesn’t release official casualty data, although Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has publicly acknowledged the scale of losses in combat. The most recent research by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimated in July that the country has endured between 525,000 and 625,000 casualties, including 125,000 and 150,000 fatalities. Alexander Baunov, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, said that the combined death toll suffered by Russia and Ukraine could exceed 1 million. Ukraine expands evacuation orders As the newly projected death toll underscores the human cost of Moscow’s war, fears are growing in Ukraine over a deteriorating security situation in the country’s eastern Donetsk region – an area mostly under Russian control – amid daily guided bomb and drone attacks . All families with children still in Donetsk were on Tuesday ordered to evacuate. Children and families in many communities in most of Ukrainian-controlled Donetsk - including the major cities of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk - were already under the evacuation order, but now the measure has been expanded to settlements further west. An estimated 64,500 civilians remain in the region as of November 2026, according to the Donetsk regional military administration. “This is an extremely difficult but necessary decision. The Russians are shelling our cities and villages every day and bombarding the region with aerial bombs,” said the head of Donetsk’s regional military administration, Vadym Filashkin. For months, Moscow’s forces have been inching towards Kramatorsk , one of Ukraine’s last strongholds in the north of Donetsk region. Tuesday’s mandatory evacuation order is a sign of Kyiv’s concern that an expansion of Russian attacks could further harm civilians and isolate communities, for example by blowing up bridges and supply routes. CNN’s Clare Sebastian, Nathan Hodge, Kosta Gak and Lauren Kent contributed reporting. item.title: DEA allowed 1.4 million fentanyl pills to reach the streets, investigation finds
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. (AP) — Federal narcotics agents monitored the fentanyl deal from every angle, staking out the parking lot and lobby of a hotel while a surveillance plane circled overhead. As the buyer arrived at 2:24 p.m. in a white pickup, the agents watched as he nonchalantly greeted a mohawked courier and entered the Home2 Suites. Eight minutes later, they exited separately into the blazing sun — one of them toting a backpack stuffed with as many as 100,000 potentially lethal counterfeit pain pills. But the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration did not pounce that Sunday in August 2024. Eight months passed before agents dismantled the major fentanyl ring flooding the Southwest as the U.S. reeled from an epidemic of opioid overdose deaths. The DEA's decision to stand down fit a pattern that would play out as agents allowed staggering amounts of fentanyl to hit the streets. The controversial tactic has sparked state and federal investigations since The Associated Press in June revealed that agents in New Mexico in recent years permitted hundreds of thousands of fentanyl pills to go unseized. At the time, the DEA denied it ever knowingly allowed the trafficking of a synthetic opioid the White House has designated a "weapon of mass destruction." That denial, however, is further contradicted by new AP findings that the DEA permitted at least 1.4 million additional pills to be trafficked between August 2024 and April 2025 as it closed in on the largest fentanyl bust in U.S. history. The AP based its tally on thousands of pages of court documents, investigative records, detailed wiretap reports and 12 hours of DEA surveillance footage. As the agents watched, the AP investigation found, dealers trafficked large packages of pills in plastic bins and duffel bags that passed through highly transited hotels, apartment complexes, Airbnb rentals and self-storage facilities in six states. The AP did not include in its tally numerous drug deals mentioned in the records that did not include specific pill counts or those that were not surveilled by the DEA. "Everybody wants the big fish, but the big fish isn't guaranteed," said Brian Besser, a former DEA senior executive who oversaw the agency's Rocky Mountain division. "When you're dealing with a substance that can take this much human life, you can't gamble like that." DEA has long allowed drugs to 'walk' The DEA at times has allowed traffickers to continue operating under strict surveillance when agents suspect they are moving cocaine, heroin and marijuana so as not to spook bigger targets — a strategy known as permitting drugs to "walk." Fentanyl, however, was supposed to be different. The drug poses such an unprecedented danger that the DEA for years ran a public safety campaign with the slogan "One Pill Can Kill." The Justice Department in 2017 began instructing agents to seize fentanyl whenever "practicable" since even unintentional contact can prove deadly. However, officials loosened those rules in 2024 to give agents more discretion even after DEA whistleblower David Howell questioned the morality and effectiveness of letting fentanyl hit the streets. "Agents are driving around in a car plastered with 'One Pill Can Kill' and at the same time walking hundreds of thousands of pills of fentanyl," said Kevin Small, a former colleague of Howell's. "They're hypocrites." The AP's reporting prompted a congressional oversight inquiry and a criminal investigation by New Mexico's attorney general amid bipartisan outrage. Even as the fentanyl crisis has subsided from its peak, it continues to batter New Mexico, where officials in Albuquerque recently declared a state of emergency and last week sued the Justice Department for $153 million in damages. Overdose deaths from the drug, much of it crudely manufactured in Mexico, spiked 44% last year in the state. "This is like trying to prevent my house from burning down by negotiating with an arsonist," New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, a Democrat, said in an interview, referring to the DEA. "They are fully engaged in the cover-up because they know they went too far and it's wrong." A DEA spokesperson declined to answer questions due to an ongoing review by the U.S. Justice Department's inspector general. The agency previously said its decisions were lawful and coordinated with federal prosecutors to prevent public harm. "Our response has not changed," DEA spokesperson Amanda Wozniak wrote in an email. The U.S. attorney's office in New Mexico and Justice Department declined to answer questions. "The Department of Justice is committed to using every lawful tool available to identify, disrupt and dismantle the organizations responsible for trafficking fentanyl into our communities," Tessa DuBerry, a U.S. attorney's office spokesperson, wrote in an emailed statement. The DEA quickly identified the distribution ring's alleged leader Defenders of DEA's wait-and-see approach have said it can lead to bigger busts and the removal of higher-ranking bosses. In this case, authorities launched an investigation in the summer of 2024 into Heriberto Salazar Amaya, the alleged leader of a trafficking ring that prosecutors say generated as much as $2 million a month in sales. The 38-year-old Mexican, who had been on the DEA's radar for a decade, was arrested in April 2025 on charges of drug trafficking and is scheduled to be tried next year. He has pleaded not guilty. His defense attorneys did not respond to requests for comment. Federal prosecutors have charged 15 other people in the case, many of them low-level couriers. A dozen of those have pleaded guilty, mostly to drug charges. None of the group's foreign suppliers in Mexico has been named. The DEA investigation was extensive and required finesse as agents eavesdropped on the network's every move. Agents set up covert cameras on residential streets and self-storage facilities, once nearly blowing the surveillance when a DEA technician stood shoulder to shoulder with a courier in the elevator of an Albuquerque Extra Space. The DEA confirmed Salazar Amaya's identity through a series of ruse calls, including one in which agents at a Las Vegas eatery secretly filmed him answering a call from a woman asking about a washer and dryer for sale. "You have the wrong number," Salazar Amaya answered before hanging up. In recordings of intercepted phone calls reviewed by AP, the soft-spoken Salazar Amaya sounded more like a switchboard operator than a cartel kingpin. Using a string of aliases and 14 phones, he can be heard taking orders and dispatching couriers to deliver large orders of drugs to major dealers from Phoenix to Denver. "I'm super stressed," Salazar Amaya told one buyer, explaining that he had gone to urgent care suffering from blurry vision and an exploding headache. Airbnb rentals played critical role in fentanyl ring Short-term rentals served as a logistical linchpin of the ring, court records show. The traffickers stayed at Airbnbs — Salazar Amaya left a public review for one — where they counted cash, stored massive bags of fentanyl pills and used digital scales to ready deliveries. The DEA frequently surveilled these residences, recording shipments from the street and a reconnaissance plane overhead. As they passed in and out of hotels and storage units, the dealers took steps to protect themselves. DEA agents found a box of N95 masks at one Airbnb, according to crime-scene photographs reviewed by AP. Several rentals used by the traffickers remain listed today. In a statement, Airbnb said it first heard from law enforcement after the dealers were arrested and was never told the investigation involved fentanyl. Experts said the DEA should have immediately alerted Airbnb and health officials so the properties could be checked for potential contamination. "It's shocking and frightening," said Michael Polkabla, an environmental hazard consultant who assists law enforcement in cleaning up fentanyl spills. "Whenever fentanyl is being handled, it's leaving significant residues." 'One pill can kill' Throughout the investigation, fentanyl reached multiple communities in New Mexico. Agents staked out a shipment of 370,000 fentanyl pills at an Albuquerque park and playground where a trafficker struggled to remove a large storage container from a vehicle. They watched as couriers driving in tandem cars ferried 200,000 pills to a home in Santa Fe's historic Agua Fria neighborhood. And they looked on as traffickers accessed a self-storage unit stocked with fentanyl nearly 500 times, tapping seemingly endless reserves of the drug. Almost all of the pills remain unaccounted for today — a loss DEA chalked up to the need to safeguard a sensitive investigation as they sought to trace the source of fentanyl to Mexico. "One small intervention on our end could cause a whole ripple effect of ruining everything," DEA Agent David Zimmerman told a federal jury last year. "You have to have a strategy on when you can stop people or take stuff off or try to intercept narcotics on these big investigations." It is not clear why the DEA decided to take down the ring when it did. When it was finished making arrests and raiding stash houses, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi touted the record bust of 4 million pills as evidence the Justice Department takes seriously the threat of fentanyl. At a May 2025 news conference, she removed a small glass vial from her pocket to emphasize the drug's unique dangers . "It looks like a few grains of salt," she said. "This is what it takes to kill you." __ Goodman reported from Miami. Associated Press journalists Susan Montoya Bryan in Albuquerque, New Mexico, and M. Reo in Washington contributed. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/ap-investigation-dea-allowed-1-110229098.html

item.title: Thanksgiving travelers are bracing for delays after a wave of airline tech outages
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The timing couldn't have been worse. Just before the busiest travel week of the year, a wave of major aviation tech outages — including a Delta Air Lines system failure on Sunday, a United Airlines disruption last Monday and a nationwide FAA ground stop on Nov. 13 — looked sure to make leaving home for Thanksgiving more stressful than ever. Suddenly, "outage anxiety" was everywhere. "I think half the country is looking at its boarding pass with suspicion," Christopher Elliott, founder of a nonprofit that helps consumers resolve travel disputes, told the New York Times . According to a YouGov poll conducted right after the ground stop , nearly three-quarters of Americans (72%) said that if they were set to fly over the holiday, they would be concerned about experiencing "flight cancellations or significant delays as a result of further disruptions to U.S. air travel." And nearly a third (31%) said the ground stop could potentially alter their plans, making them less likely to travel by air for Thanksgiving. AAA projects nearly 6 million people will fly domestically over the seven-day Thanksgiving travel period. But now that the digital chaos seems to have subsided and Americans are starting to hit the road, how worried should you really be about additional meltdowns snarling your holiday travel plans? The simple answer: We don't know. An outage is, by definition, unexpected. The FAA said it was forced to ground thousands of flights after a router installed during a copper-to-fiber network upgrade flooded its telecommunications network with excessive data, overwhelming legacy equipment and destabilizing radar and communications feeds. Delta's outage was traced to a "database issue" in its automated weight-and-balance system. United's outage was similar. None were the result of a cyberattack, officials insisted. But none were foreseen, either. "This has never happened," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CBS News , referring to the chain of events that triggered the ground stop. "And so that's why … we felt comfortable doing [the upgrade] in the middle of the day — because it's been done thousands of times. We've never had this situation." On Nov. 16, the Trump administration convened a "tiger team" — a small group of experts or specialists who work together on solving a specific problem that isn't easily addressed by normal operations — to prevent similar outages going forward. Composed of officials from the FAA, the Transportation Department, the Defense Department and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the team has "met every day this week to ensure continuity of service," according to the Daily Wire . A White House spokesperson said Americans preparing to travel for Thanksgiving have nothing to worry about, the outlet added. "President Trump and Secretary Duffy have brought together the best and the brightest across the government to ensure what happened [on Nov. 13] can never happen again," the spokesperson said. "Work continues, and Americans can rest assured their country's aviation is the best in the world." Why tech upgrades can cause outages But even if travelers survive the Thanksgiving rush without major incident, the experts suggest that future outages are simply inevitable . According to Microsoft President and Vice Chair Brad Smith — whose own company suffered a massive global outage earlier this month — AI is the common thread here, even if it didn't directly cause any of the recent travel disruptions. "What AI did earlier this year was basically make it much easier for people to find vulnerabilities in code, and then you can either use that knowledge to patch the code, or if you're a bad actor, you can use that knowledge to try to hack into systems," he told CBS News on Sunday . Smith went on to say that organizations are now rushing to patch vulnerabilities "at a pace we have never seen before" —a rush that itself creates instability, particularly within legacy systems. "Especially when you have older infrastructure, especially when you're trying to patch at such a pace, especially when you have to go so fast that you can't take as much time to test what you're changing in the code, you do increase the risk of something going wrong," he explained. The bottom line? Americans "have to be prepared" for more disruptions in "the coming months because this isn't the type of thing that just gets done in a couple of weeks," Smith said. "The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now." Even as the White House tries to reassure Thanksgiving travelers, administration officials have predicted that more outages are on the way. "The American people should understand that a great deal of our digital infrastructure is dated. It is old. It has been built out over three decades or more. We are in a period of technological step change, both in terms of what people refer to as [AI] models, applications, and the like, and in computing power," Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNN on Sunday . "And in that technological step change, our systems are going to need to be upgraded," Clayton continued. "They're going to need to be upgraded for performance and for cybersecurity. And as part of that ongoing upgrade, we are going to have glitches, gaps, interruptions in service. That is going to happen." Asked if "the American people" should "just be prepared for more outages" because of those upgrades, Clayton effectively said yes. "They should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road," Clayton said. "Any time you refurbish your house, upgrade any of your systems, there are going to be things that you do not expect." How to prepare With that in mind, it's probably wise to plan for the worst if you're leaving home for the holiday — especially if you're flying. Print everything: boarding passes, visas and so on. Forgo checked bags, if possible. (Or at least track your luggage.) Keep your receipts. And know your rights : Transportation Department rules require airlines to issue a refund if your flight is canceled or significantly delayed for any reason (assuming you decline a replacement ticket or travel credit). After all, outages aren’t the only obstacle to consider this weekend. Major storms are also set to strike both coasts — including one that could last through Thanksgiving Day — and record-challenging king tides are threatening coastal flooding from California to Florida as a result of El Niño . item.title: Judge pushed back on DOJ over search of Ilhan Omar's home, court records show
item.description:

WASHINGTON (AP) — A magistrate judge who authorized a recent search of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar 's home by federal agents ruled that the Minnesota Democrat was entitled to assert her right to privacy protections afforded to sitting members of Congress at the outset of the search, according to court documents unsealed on Monday. The unsealed filings reveal how Justice Department attorneys and U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh resolved their initial disagreement over the thorny constitutional implications of searching a member of Congress’ private residence for a criminal investigation. The heavily redacted documents — released in response to a lawsuit filed by media organizations — do not appear to shed new light on the reason or outcome of the search itself or disclose new details of an immigration-fraud investigation that Omar claims is politically motivated. Federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork and have issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives, The Associated Press reported last month, citing a person briefed on the investigation who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation. The unsealed filings show that Sharbaugh — before authorizing the search of Omar's home — raised concerns about the “Speech or Debate Clause” implications of searching a private residence belonging to a member of Congress. The clause, which is designed to protect legislators from executive branch interference or intimidation, includes a privilege against compelled disclosures. Sharbaugh said he disagreed with the government's argument that the privilege is limited only to official congressional offices and certain electronic devices. “That logic does not hold,” the magistrate wrote. Sharbaugh concluded that the government's law-enforcement interests needed to be balanced against Omar's constitutional rights as a member of Congress. He said the government ultimately agreed to a search protocol allowing Omar to invoke a privilege over any Speech or Debate Clause material before agents carried out the search. Omar, a naturalized U.S. citizen born in Somalia, has been a target of anti-immigrant rhetoric by President Donald Trump and many Republican allies. She hasn’t been charged with any crimes and has denied any wrongdoing. Chief Judge James Boasberg ordered the partial unsealing of court filings related to the Oct. 12 search of Omar’s Washington, D.C., home by Department of Homeland Security agents. He ruled after over a dozen news organizations, including The Associated Press, argued that the public has a First Amendment right to access the records. Boasberg agreed with the government that it would be premature to unseal a 67-page search warrant affidavit containing sensitive details of the government’s investigation. In a court filing last month, the government argued that it would jeopardize the investigation to unseal the court records before a charging decision is made. An attorney for Omar didn't immediately respond to an email seeking comment Monday on the unsealed documents. Agents conducted the court-authorized search less than a month before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Omar won her reelection bid. The Justice Department historically has avoided public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of an election. Omar has said DHS agents seized 17 items , including phones, notebooks, a Somali-language children’s book and a vintage camera that her husband had received as a gift. ___ Associated Press writer Alanna Durkin Richer contributed to this report. item.title: Chinese tech giant convicted in sweeping U.S. criminal case over its business in Iran
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Karen Freifeld NEW YORK, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Chinese telecommunications equipment maker Huawei was convicted by a jury in New York City on Tuesday in a sprawling US criminal case on charges that it deceived banks about its business in Iran and stole trade secrets from American companies. The verdict came ‌in a criminal case that began in 2018, with the US government the following year placing Huawei on a trade blacklist that restricted its access ‌to US technology amid American concerns that Huawei posed national security risks. The jury in Brooklyn federal court found Huawei guilty on 10 of the 12 criminal counts the company faced, including bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions ​violations and conspiring to steal trade secrets. The jury acquitted Huawei of conspiring to obstruct justice and racketeering conspiracy, a charge alleging the company had acted as a criminal enterprise. The trial lasted more than two months, with prosecutors calling more than 60 witnesses and the defense calling 15. It was not immediately clear what penalties Huawei will face when US District Judge Ann Donnelly sentences it on September 14, 2027. Reuters stories in 2012 and 2013 helped expose Huawei's activities in Iran and were discussed during the trial. "After the media started questioning Huawei's operations in ‌Iran, so did Huawei's banks," prosecutor Meredith Arfa told jurors during ⁠closing arguments in the case last week. Brian Heberlig, a lawyer for Huawei, said the company was disappointed by the convictions but said the acquittal on the racketeering conspiracy charge vindicated its "good-faith compliance culture." "We fully expect to appeal," Heberlig told reporters. US Attorney Joseph Nocella said in a ⁠statement: “Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering US national security, violating the sanctity of US commerce, and impeding the enforcement of US laws.” China's embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Asked how much the company may have to pay in penalties, Heberlig said it was premature to comment, but said the acquittal on the racketeering conspiracy charge could make ​a ​significant difference. Experts have said the case did not undermine Huawei's business, as the company diversified and emerged ​as a key player in China's push for artificial intelligence. FOUNDER'S DAUGHTER ‌WAS DETAINED In December 2018, Meng Wanzhou, Huawei's chief financial officer and daughter of the company's founder, was detained in Canada on a US warrant, prompting a diplomatic crisis involving the United States, China and Canada. Meng had been secretly indicted on US charges of misleading an HSBC banker about Huawei's business in Iran, so the company could move dollars in and out of Iran in violation of American sanctions. Meng fought extradition to the US for nearly three years, before entering a deferred prosecution agreement and flying home to China to a hero's welcome. The charges against her were dropped. Meng did not testify at trial, though an HSBC banker she met with in 2013 did testify. The 2018 indictment alleged that Huawei misled ‌HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas about its business dealings in Iran. Prosecutors added new charges ​in 2020, including allegations that Huawei conspired to steal trade secrets from US technology companies over two decades. Jurors watched a video that, according to prosecutors, showed a Huawei ​employee slipping a piece of a T-Mobile ​testing robot into his backpack, and heard about a Huawei engineer sneaking into a Fujitsu booth at a trade show to photograph a device. Prosecutors gave jurors a statement attached to Meng's deferred prosecution agreement in which she acknowledged that the company illegally conducted business in Iran. The defense argued that HSBC and the other banks ​knew about Huawei's business in Iran and were competing for ‌Huawei's business. Heberlig accused prosecutors during his closing argument of having "cherry-picked" a handful of disparate incidents to support their claim of a 20-year conspiracy. Heberlig said ​Huawei succeeded through "hard work, innovation, and investment in research and development." The company has more than 200,000 employees and operates in approximately 170 countries. item.title: Feds call for evacuations before Iowa munition detonation
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The U.S. Army on Tuesday called for evacuations after it defended its plan to detonate 68 barrels of toxic lead-based explosives stored at a facility in Iowa — despite concerns from environmental groups — following approval from a federal appeals court. At a press conference at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said there is a consensus among experts that "a controlled, mitigated detonation" of the entire U.S. stockpile of lead azide "is far preferable for public safety than an uncontrolled detonation." "Inaction is no longer an option," added Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, the Army's leader of the operation. The planned detonation is scheduled for Wednesday morning at 9 a.m. local time. The Army has recommended that all residents of Middletown and the immediate surrounding areas evacuate starting Tuesday "out of an abundance of caution." The Federal Emergency Management Agency is offering transportation and safe lodging for residents who are unable to evacuate on their own. Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds backed the Army's decision on Thursday, writing on social media that she has asked for as much information as possible to prepare the surrounding area for the blast. "I believe, based on the information I've been given, that the danger is immediate, and I trust the Army will do everything in its power to protect the people who could be affected," she wrote on X . The announcement followed a judgment from the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals on Monday, which said the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency had "adequately incorporated safeguards to minimize the dispersal of lead dust." The ruling acknowledged the detonation presented "real risks," but concluded that "we must acknowledge the realities of the situation: the degraded explosives present a risk of an uncontrolled and unplanned explosion, which would occur without the benefit of the safety measures that the Permit puts in place." The court's decision came hours after President Trump announced that he had halted the plan. In a Truth Social post , Trump said that while he believes the "proper course is to get rid of this long-term problem," he would not allow the Army to destroy the material until federal courts sign off on the plan and Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand gives his approval. Sand, who takes office in January, has said the decision is up to the Trump administration "based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago." The explosion threatens to send a plume of toxic lead dust over local communities, livestock and farmland in the surrounding area. A map depicting the likely range of airborne lead dust from the planned detonation, released Nov. 24. U.S. Army "The detonation is expected to produce a dust plume containing lead particles that may travel beyond the installation and settle on surrounding surfaces," the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency warned in a statement on Tuesday . Environmentalists sued to stop the detonation last week, setting off a back-and-forth legal battle. The military has argued that the controlled detonation must take place soon, before impending cold weather potentially causes the material to combust on its own. Here's what led to the current situation, what the dangers are and what might happen next. How did we get here? The roots of the controversy reportedly date back to at least March, when the Army discovered nearly 5 tons of deteriorating lead azide, a dangerous bomb-making material, stored at an ammunition plant in rural Iowa. According to legal filings , the lead azide had crystallized over the course of two decades, leaving it highly susceptible to exploding. The material is so volatile, the Army says, that the friction and motion of moving it somewhere safer would likely cause it to explode. According to the New York Times, the Army originally hired a chemical company to neutralize the material without an explosion, but later determined that detonating it was the right course of action. Earlier this month, the Environmental Protection Agency approved an emergency permit allowing the Army to carry out a controlled detonation of the lead azide. The detonation was initially scheduled to take place on Friday. But local environmental groups filed a lawsuit aiming to stop the plan from going forward, arguing that the EPA failed to apply proper environmental standards when it approved the detonation, creating the risk of "immediate, irreparable harm" to surrounding communities. On Thursday, a federal appeals court issued an order temporarily blocking the Army from carrying out the detonation. But the Army argued in a filing Saturday that the situation has become so dangerous that it has the authority to proceed under a separate emergency exemption. The blast was on track to happen on Wednesday until Trump intervened. The court issued its ruling allowing the detonation to proceed about five hours after Trump's post was published. What are the risks? Lead is a neurotoxin that poses a serious risk to those who are exposed to it, particularly pregnant women and young children. No one disputes that blowing up the barrels of lead azide could release dangerous material to the surrounding area. The Army shared modeling showing lead particles from the explosion traveling as far as 40 miles and airborne dust drifting up to 100 miles. The American Lung Association has advised people in the area to stay indoors for 24 to 48 hours after the blast to avoid exposure. The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services recommended residents take additional precautions, including turning off their home's air conditioning and heating systems, washing outdoor surfaces covered in visible dust with soap and water and washing hands before eating. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention announced Thursday that it has mobilized to assist the state in its monitoring and response after the detonation takes place. The Army argues that, whatever risks the planned detonation poses, doing nothing creates the danger of something much worse. An aerial view shows homes in Middletown, Iowa, on Nov. 20. Scott Olson/Getty Images "The real choice … is not between a detonation and no detonation," the government wrote in a legal filing . "It is between a planned and mitigated detonation and an unplanned and unmitigated explosion." But environmental groups have countered that the public was only given a few days' notice before the initial planned detonation, not nearly enough time for local residents to understand the full scope of the risk and take the steps they need to stay safe. The groups also questioned how the Army allowed the situation to become so urgent when it had been aware of the material for at least eight months. Sand echoed that sentiment in a post on social media on Sunday. "No good options exist and the situation is more dangerous and unpredictable than it ever should have been," he wrote on X . "Most clearly, since a contract to remove explosive risk was signed this spring, we must all be asking why it was cancelled, why nothing was done, and why we are rushing to demolition now in late November." item.title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia plans to fly to Spain after months of U.S. deportation efforts
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the El Salvador native who was mistakenly deported last year and sent to a notorious prison in his home country, is planning to leave the U.S. for Spain on Tuesday, according to multiple U.S. officials familiar with the matter. Abrego Garcia, whose case became an early flashpoint in the debate over the Trump administration's deportation crackdown, is set to fly to Spain on a commercial flight Tuesday, according to the sources, who requested anonymity to talk about an arrangement that has not been disclosed publicly. The exact nature of his arrangements and the conditions of his departure from the U.S. were not immediately clear. But the federal judge in Maryland overseeing his civil legal case issued an order Friday that remains sealed. CBS News has reached out to an attorney and representatives for Abrego Garcia. The move by Abrego Garcia comes after the Trump administration spent months trying to deport the man, who came to the U.S. illegally 15 years ago and had been living in Maryland with his wife and children when he was detained by immigration authorities in March 2025. He was then deported to El Salvador and held for months in the country's CECOT prison, despite a previous court order barring him from being sent back to his home country. He was brought back to the United States last year to face criminal charges. Abrego Garcia has maintained for more than a year that if he had to leave the U.S. again, he would be willing to go to Costa Rica, and designated the Central American nation as his preferred country of removal. But the Trump administration had resisted that suggestion and instead unsuccessfully sought to deport Abrego Garcia to numerous African countries, including Uganda, Eswatini and Ghana. In more recent months, the Department of Homeland Security said it was ready to deport Abrego Garcia to Liberia — part of a broader practice of sending deportees to countries in Africa. Abrego Garcia's departure from the U.S. came weeks after a hearing before U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis, who has been presiding over a civil case stemming from his deportation last year, was abruptly cancelled . The judge ordered Immigration and Customs Enforcement last year to release Abrego Garcia from immigration custody and has continued to bar immigration authorities from detaining him while litigation continued. But the Trump administration had sought to lift Xinis' orders, which it said were the only impediments to Abrego Garcia's "prompt removal." The Justice Department said in March that the government was "ready, willing, and able" to deport Abrego Garcia to Liberia in West Africa. Abrego Garcia's case gained national prominence last year after a top administration official acknowledged that his removal to El Salvador was an "error." Following his arrest by immigration authorities in March 2025, Abrego Garcia was among the more than 200 immigrants who were sent to El Salvador and detained at its notorious supermax prison, the Terrorism Confinement Center, or CECOT. But Abrego Garcia had been granted a withholding of removal by an immigration judge in 2019, which prevented immigration authorities from deporting him to his home country of El Salvador because he was at risk of persecution by local gangs. In April 2025, Xinis ordered the Department of Homeland Security to bring Abrego Garcia back to the U.S., and the Supreme Court said the government had to facilitate his release from Salvadoran custody. The Trump administration ultimately brought Abrego Garcia back to the U.S. in June 2025, but only after he was indicted on federal charges of human smuggling stemming from a 2022 traffic stop in Tennessee. Abrego Garcia pleaded not guilty and in May, a federal judge in Tennessee dismissed the criminal charges on the grounds that his prosecution was vindictive. The Justice Department has appealed that decision , and arguments before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit are scheduled for February. item.title: Trump administration eyes tariff hikes on 16 trading partners after Supreme Court setback
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Trump administration will propose new tariff hikes Tuesday night on the European Union, China, Mexico, Japan and 12 other trading partners, a major step towards recreating the president’s global duties the Supreme Court struck down in February. According to one person with knowledge of the planning, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer will announce the new tariff proposals as part of a report into the countries’ excess manufacturing capacity. The findings are the product of a trade investigation Greer’s office launched in March under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the U.S. trade representative to impose tariffs in response to unfair trade practices. Three other people briefed by the administration on the investigation confirmed the report was in the process of being finalized and the results would be announced as soon as today. They were granted anonymity to share details of policy plans that are not yet public. The Wall Street Journal first reported the announcement was coming. The person with knowledge said the proposed new duties will honor the tariff ceilings countries have negotiated with the Trump administration over the past year, in exchange for trade concessions and massive investment in American industries. China’s overall tariff rate, for example, won’t exceed 20%, while the EU’s will stay below the 15% cap that the president agreed to with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Turnberry, Scotland in 2025. Targeted countries will still have an opportunity to weigh in through hearings, public comments and closed-door talks for the rates are finalized. Like other recent tariff hikes, the new duties are also expected to come with a raft of carve-outs. And there will be an opportunity for future tariff reductions if countries take steps to reduce their manufacturing overcapacity, the person with knowlege said. But the threat of further tariffs, alone, is likely to enrage foreign allies already frustrated by other elements of Trump’s trade policies they believe violate their existing agreements. In its filing in March, Greer’s office said there is evidence countries like China have aggressively expanded their production in strategic sectors beyond what demand can support and said the country, alongside other partners like the European Union, maintains a global goods surplus. The investigation is the second of two sweeping trade probes launched in the spring as part of the Trump administration’s mission to rebuild its tariff regime after the "reciprocal" duties he imposed in 2025 were invalidated. The administration completed an investigation into forced labor in foreign supply chains over the summer, which it said justified tariffs of between 10 and 12.5 percent on dozens of trading partners, including all 16 of the economies covered by the excess manufacturing probe. Any tariffs that are ultimately imposed following the excess manufacturing investigation would stack on top of those existing tariff rates. Higher tariffs risks complicating delicate relationships with major economies and come amid a fragile trade truce with China that expires in January. Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping are set to meet during the G20 summit next month. It also comes amid tense negotiations with Mexico over the renewal of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement. Like Trump’s other efforts to impose tariffs after his Supreme Court defeat, any new duties the government imposes based on this investigation are likely to be challenged in court. The administration’s forced labor tariffs are currently under scrutiny at the U.S. Court of International Trade. Stefanie Bolzen contributed to this report.
